translation: O wife, my wife, may dust fall in people's eyes, O wife, my wife; O wife, my wife, they could not bear to see us, could they, O wife, my wife; O wife, my wife, they slipped us a secret potion and turned us apart, didn't they, O wife, my darling wife; O wife, my darling wife

Before we were married, the two of us went roaming around together calling 'Sengo pilla'; went roaming around calling 'Sengo pilla'. They fixed their eyes on us, ganged up, and tried to light a fire and wreck our wedding; tried to light a fire and wreck our wedding. When we were married and living together, they could not bear it and burned up with jealousy, didn't they, O wife, my wife; they put on all kinds of false faces, didn't they, O wife, my wife

Some she-demon latched on to me before I knew it and turned my heart away from you; turned my heart away from you. Wicked people gave you a potion and killed your love for me; killed your love for me. Seeing us living happily together, they nursed a grudge and stirred up a fire, didn't they, O wife, my wife; they pushed it as far as divorce papers, didn't they, O wife, my wife

In the first days of our marriage, whenever Sunday came, we would bring home half a seer of arrack; we would bring home half a seer of arrack. Shutting the doors and sitting in the middle of the house, the two of us would drink together all day long; the two of us would drink together all day long. We would cook a two-kilo chicken and eat it with relish for two meals, O wife, my wife; we would chat together until dawn, wouldn't we, O wife, my wife

Useless at labouring work, I sat around and ate, and you never said a word; I sat around and ate, and you never said a word. When I craved toddy and asked you for small change, you put it straight in my hands; when I asked for small change, you put it straight in my hands. When I lost money at card games and wailed, you comforted me, didn't you, O wife, my wife; you cared for me like your own life, O wife, my darling wife

Chee, chee, may my mouth that cursed you rot away, may my hands that beat you wither; may my hands that beat you wither. Listening to other people's talk, I tormented you terribly and tried to hang you; tormented you terribly and tried to hang you. With these sinful hands of mine I covered your back in welts, O wife, my wife; blind drunk, I cracked your head open, O wife, my darling wife

Since you sulked and stayed on at your mother's house, my life has become like a beggar's; my life has become like a beggar's. Ever since you left me and came here, I have lived a dog's misery with no one to turn to; a dog's misery with no one to turn to. From now on I won't drink, from now on I won't roam around, so forgive me now and come home, O wife, my wife; let us live together sensibly, O wife, my wife; let us stay together without becoming the talk of the town, O wife, my wife; let us live together sensibly, O wife, my wife
summaryEn:
In this family song a husband pleads with his wife, whom he calls 'penlama' (wife), to forgive him and come home. The pallavi and the first two verses blame outsiders: envious people who could not bear their love, who tried to break up the match before the wedding, and who, he believes, slipped them a secret potion ('marugu mandu') that turned them against each other until things went as far as divorce papers. The song draws on the common village belief that jealousy and charms can spoil a marriage.

The mood then turns to nostalgia and confession. He remembers their early married Sundays, drinking arrack behind closed doors, sharing a chicken and talking till dawn, and admits that she fed him while he sat idle, gave him money for toddy and consoled him after he lost at cards. In the fifth verse he confesses cursing her, beating her, leaving welts on her back and cracking her head while drunk, and curses his own hands. Now she has gone back to her mother's house, and he promises to give up drinking and wandering. The frank picture of alcohol and domestic violence sits alongside the humour of a folk lament. Each verse repeats its half-lines and closes on the refrain 'O penlama naa penlama'.
summaryTe:
ఈ కుటుంబ గీతంలో ఒక భర్త తన భార్యను 'ఓ పెండ్లామా' అని పిలుస్తూ, తనను క్షమించి ఇంటికి తిరిగి రమ్మని వేడుకుంటాడు. పల్లవిలోనూ మొదటి రెండు చరణాల్లోనూ అతను నిందను బయటి వాళ్ళ మీదే వేస్తాడు: తమ ప్రేమను చూసి ఓర్వలేని మంది, పెళ్ళికి ముందే చిచ్చుపెట్టి పెళ్ళి చెడగొట్టాలని చూసినవాళ్ళు, మరుగు మందు పెట్టి ఇద్దరి మనసులు మార్చి ఇడుపు కాగితాల దాకా తెచ్చినవాళ్ళు. అసూయ, మందు మాయలు కాపురాన్ని చెడగొడతాయనే పల్లె నమ్మకం ఇక్కడ కనిపిస్తుంది.

ఆ తర్వాత పాట జ్ఞాపకాల, ఒప్పుకోలు స్వరంలోకి మారుతుంది. పెళ్ళైన కొత్తలో ఆదివారం తలుపులేసుకుని సారా తాగడం, కోడికూర వండుకుని తినడం, తెల్లవారే దాకా ముచ్చట్లాడుకోవడం గుర్తుచేసుకుంటాడు. తాను పని చేయకుండా కూర్చుని తిన్నా ఆమె ఏమీ అనలేదని, కల్లుకు చిల్లర ఇచ్చిందని, పేకాటలో పైసలు పోగొట్టుకున్నప్పుడు ఓదార్చిందని ఒప్పుకుంటాడు. ఐదో చరణంలో ఆమెను తిట్టినందుకు, తాగి కొట్టి వీపు నిండా వాతలు పెట్టినందుకు, తల పగలగొట్టినందుకు తన నోరు, చేతులు పడిపోవాలని తనను తానే శపించుకుంటాడు. ఇప్పుడు ఆమె అవ్వగారింట్లో ఉండగా, ఇక తాగనని, తిరగనని మాట ఇచ్చి నలుగురిలో పడకుండా కలిసి ఉందామని బతిమాలుతాడు. తాగుడు, గృహ హింస వంటి విషయాలను దాచకుండా చూపిస్తూనే, జానపద విలాపంలోని హాస్యాన్నీ ఈ పాట కలుపుకుంటుంది. ప్రతి చరణంలో పాదాలు రెండుసార్లు పాడబడి, 'ఓ పెండ్లామా నా పెండ్లామా' అనే పల్లవి మాటతో ముగుస్తాయి.
